brief: Stock-to-stock correlation is at or near an all-time low even as common-factor risks from higher yields and higher yield volatility are rising, per Bloomberg strategist Simon White. Yields remain at levels not seen in over 20 years, yet the S&P is near all-time highs with the VIX near 15. Low index correlation explains the gap: single-stock volatility is relatively elevated, but low correlation dampens the VIX. Six-month realised correlation hit a series low (data since 2011), likely an all-time low, at 5.2%; implied correlation is near but not at its record low. Yield volatility had been falling even as yields rose, since the rise was read as stabilising, driven by inflation-dampening short-rate tightening. Since Wednesday's strong PMI data, yield vol has started rising as the move turns more disorderly. Strong growth combined with a large pro-cyclical deficit deemed inappropriate for this stage of the cycle, plus heavy AI-related spending, intensifies inflation risk, raising the odds of a yield shock that would push stocks to fall together, i.e. become more correlated. Current correlation levels look backward-looking and are not yet pricing that rising common-factor risk.
